Trying to Conceive

What unexplained infertility means

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Unexplained infertility means that the usual assessment has not found a clear reason pregnancy has not happened. Normal results can feel frustrating when the outcome you want is still missing. The diagnosis describes a limit in what has been identified so far; it does not make your experience imaginary, prove that every step of reproduction is normal or mean that there are no options.

Check what the diagnosis is based on

A useful explanation starts with the actual investigations, not just the word unexplained. The assessment usually considers ovulation, the uterus and fallopian tubes, and semen. Where two partners are contributing eggs and sperm, both need appropriate evaluation rather than focusing exclusively on one person.

Ask for a summary showing which tests were done, the dates and the findings. If a key part of the initial assessment is missing, the label may be premature. Equally, not having every available test does not automatically mean your care is incomplete. The clinician should explain why the standard findings support the diagnosis and whether your history suggests anything more specific.

Ovulation, tubes, uterus and semen answer different questions

A menstrual history can suggest whether ovulation is occurring, with additional tests when needed. A tubal test checks whether contrast can pass through the fallopian tubes. Ultrasound can assess pelvic anatomy, including some uterine abnormalities. Semen analysis examines features such as sperm number, movement and shape.

These are useful findings, but none is a complete fertility certificate. Open tubes do not prove that every transport function works perfectly; a reassuring scan does not show all microscopic conditions. A semen result within reference ranges does not guarantee fertilization. Ask what each result establishes and what it cannot tell you.

Surgery is not a mandatory final box to tick

Hysteroscopy uses a camera to examine the uterine cavity, while laparoscopy looks inside the pelvis through abdominal incisions. They can be valuable for selected concerns, but neither is automatically required before unexplained infertility can be discussed.

An abnormal scan, significant pain, previous infection or surgery may change the balance of benefits and risks. If a procedure is proposed, ask what is suspected and how finding it would alter treatment. If it is not proposed, ask why. A careful assessment can use the least invasive useful approach without pretending that all uncertainty has disappeared.

Unexplained and idiopathic can describe different situations

Idiopathic means that the cause is unknown, but clinical terms are used in context. For example, a clinician may describe idiopathic male infertility when semen findings are abnormal and the reason for that abnormality has not been established. That differs from a couple whose standard semen and other initial assessments are reassuring.

Similarly, identifying an ovulation disorder is a finding even if its underlying cause remains uncertain. Avoid interpreting a label as proof that one partner is responsible or that a particular result makes conception impossible. Ask the clinician to explain the terminology used in your report and what practical difference it makes.

Ovarian reserve is not the same as egg quality

Tests such as anti-Müllerian hormone, or AMH, and an antral follicle count help estimate how the ovaries may respond to stimulation. They do not directly inspect every egg’s capacity to fertilize and develop. A good reserve result is not a mandatory certificate that all eggs are healthy, and a lower result does not automatically mean natural conception is impossible.

Age remains important when discussing fertility and treatment. During IVF, laboratory observations of retrieved eggs provide additional information, but appearance alone cannot fully establish developmental or chromosomal potential. Ask how reserve results influence a treatment decision rather than treating one number as your entire prognosis.

Sperm function goes beyond a routine count

Routine semen testing is important because it can identify a low count or problems with movement and shape. Results can vary, and an abnormal sample may need confirmation and further assessment. Some aspects of sperm function and genetic material are not directly measured by a routine analysis.

That gap does not mean everyone needs a sperm DNA-fragmentation test. Current guidance questions routine use and the benefit of many interventions offered after a high result. Age and health can influence sperm, but a normal-looking sample or an isolated DNA result cannot explain every failed cycle or predict a future child’s health. Ask whether an extra test would change an evidence-based decision.

Endometriosis may deserve a targeted discussion

Endometriosis can affect fertility and may occur with pelvic pain, painful periods, pain during sex or bowel symptoms. Ovarian endometriomas and some deeper disease can be visible on imaging. A normal ultrasound does not rule out all endometriosis, particularly superficial disease.

This is a reason to take symptoms seriously, not a reason to assume that every unexplained case has hidden endometriosis. The role of surgery depends on symptoms, likely findings, age, ovarian reserve and the fertility plan. Discuss the potential benefit alongside the risks and the time involved. Once a relevant condition is diagnosed, the care plan can be reconsidered in that context.

General health and celiac disease can be relevant

Tell the fertility team about diabetes, thyroid disease, autoimmune illness, digestive symptoms and medicines, including conditions managed by another clinician. A targeted investigation can be appropriate when history or symptoms suggest a problem. Broad immune testing without a specific indication is a different matter and is not a routine answer to unexplained infertility.

Celiac disease is one condition worth discussing: current NICE guidance says blood testing can be considered in unexplained subfertility. Studies give differing estimates of how often it occurs, so a single older claim of a sixfold increase should not be treated as everyone’s risk. Do not start a gluten-free diet before discussing testing, because removing gluten can affect diagnostic results.

Cervical mucus is not a simple pass-or-fail barrier

After intercourse, sperm travel through the cervix and reproductive tract. Problems such as cervical narrowing or infection may warrant assessment when suspected. Older explanations sometimes describe hostile mucus or antibodies preventing sperm from progressing, but that wording can imply more certainty than the evidence supports.

A postcoital test examines mucus after intercourse. It is not recommended as a routine fertility investigation because it does not reliably guide prognosis or care. Routine antisperm-antibody testing is also not advised. Ask about a specific suspected condition rather than accepting an unvalidated mucus test as the missing answer.

Implantation and the uterine lining remain complex

An embryo must reach a suitable uterine environment and implant for a pregnancy to continue. Fibroids, polyps or other abnormalities may be assessed when indicated, but a failed cycle does not automatically prove that the lining rejected a healthy embryo.

A biopsy or a commercially marketed receptivity result may sound as though it measures the exact missing step. Before paying for it, ask whether the test has been shown to guide treatment that improves live birth for someone in your situation. A plausible biological mechanism and an actionable clinical test are not the same thing.

A viral association is not an established treatment target

One small 2016 study examined HHV-6A, a herpesvirus, in endometrial tissue. It detected viral DNA in some women with unexplained infertility and not in the comparison group. This was a research observation about a possible association, not proof that the virus caused those fertility difficulties.

The finding did not establish that routine biopsies, viral screening or antiviral treatment improve the chance of a baby. Similar caution applies to claims about immune cells or the uterine microbiome. If a test is offered on this basis, ask whether it is research, what outcome evidence exists and what harms or costs are involved.

Luteal phase deficiency has important diagnostic limits

The luteal phase follows ovulation, when progesterone helps prepare and support the uterine lining. The idea of luteal phase deficiency has been proposed as an explanation for some fertility problems. However, a single progesterone result or a short phase does not provide a reliable diagnosis of why pregnancy has not occurred.

ASRM’s updated opinion notes the lack of a dependable test that distinguishes fertile from infertile people in this setting and the lack of proven natural-cycle treatment benefit. That is different from progesterone prescribed as part of a fertility-treatment protocol. Do not start, stop or reinterpret prescribed support on the basis of this general discussion.

Fertilization and embryo development can reveal more information

Even when sperm and eggs meet, fertilization and later cell division do not always proceed as expected. IVF allows the laboratory to observe steps that are usually hidden inside the body, such as whether eggs fertilize and how embryos develop.

Those observations may help plan another treatment, but they do not always identify one underlying cause. Poor development can involve several factors, and a visually promising embryo is not a guaranteed pregnancy. IVF is a treatment with costs, burdens and risks; it should not be presented as a simple diagnostic test that will necessarily solve the mystery.

Pregnancy without treatment is possible, but not predictable from one study

Some people diagnosed with infertility later conceive without treatment. In a 2012 Australian observational study, 1,376 women reported a history of infertility; 43.8% of the untreated group subsequently reported a birth. The study involved women aged twenty-eight to thirty-six and was not limited to people with a confirmed unexplained-infertility diagnosis.

That result is not a personal success rate, a monthly chance or evidence that treatment should be delayed for everyone. Age, how long you have been trying, prior pregnancies and clinical findings matter. Conception is not certain in any one cycle, but describing prolonged difficulty as mere bad luck can overlook a need for timely care.

Agree on the next step and when to review it

A plan may include a defined period of trying without treatment, ovarian stimulation combined with intrauterine insemination, or IVF. Insemination places prepared sperm in the uterus; IVF involves fertilizing retrieved eggs in the laboratory. Treatment can be useful without identifying one exact cause.

Guidelines and local pathways differ on timing and the preferred sequence. For example, NICE’s 2026 pathway discusses stimulated insemination or IVF after its defined period of trying and does not recommend ovarian stimulation alone for unexplained infertility. Your clinic should explain the recommendation for you, likely live-birth outcomes, multiple-pregnancy and stimulation risks, costs and a review point. A general pathway should not become an instruction to wait indefinitely.

Seek clarification without dismissing your experience

Assessment is commonly offered after twelve months of trying, with earlier evaluation for older age, irregular cycles or another known concern. If you have already had an assessment, new symptoms or a substantial passage of time can justify revisiting the plan. You do not have to wait for a routine deadline when a clinician has identified a reason to act sooner.

A second opinion can help check whether the investigations and proposed approach fit your situation, although it cannot promise a newly discovered cause. Counseling or peer support can make uncertainty easier to carry alongside medical care. You deserve a clear explanation and shared decisions; emotional support is not a claim that relaxing will cure infertility.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

ASRM, ESHRE and NICE support a defined initial assessment and selective use of additional investigations.

Current guidance cautions against several marketed tests that do not reliably improve treatment decisions or outcomes.

How BeMama can help

Keep previous results, symptom notes and questions together for your appointment. Tracking can support a conversation but cannot establish the cause of infertility.

When to seek help

Seek timely assessment when age, irregular cycles, significant pain or known reproductive conditions make earlier care appropriate. New severe symptoms require their own evaluation.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Unexplained infertility is a meaningful description of current findings, not a dismissal.
  • Standard tests cover ovulation, reproductive anatomy and semen without measuring every step.
  • Reserve, sperm DNA and uterine-lining tests have limits; more testing is not always more useful.
  • Research associations and older success figures should not become personal diagnoses or promises.
  • Agree on individualized options, expected benefits, risks and a review date.

Frequently asked questions

Does unexplained mean nothing physical is wrong?

No. It means the standard assessment has not identified a clear explanation; not every reproductive process can be measured directly.

Must everyone have hysteroscopy or laparoscopy?

No. These procedures need a clinical reason and discussion of whether the result would change care.

Does a normal AMH result prove my eggs are good quality?

No. AMH is mainly useful for anticipating ovarian response to treatment, not certifying egg quality or guaranteeing natural conception.

Can endometriosis be present after a normal scan?

Yes. Discuss suggestive symptoms, but do not assume every unexplained case has hidden endometriosis.

Should I stop gluten to improve fertility?

Discuss celiac testing first if appropriate. A gluten-free diet is not a general treatment for unexplained infertility and can interfere with diagnostic testing.

Do I automatically need sperm DNA testing?

No. Ask what the result would change and what evidence supports that action. Routine testing and many follow-on treatments have important evidence limitations.

Does a uterine virus study justify antiviral treatment?

No. A small association study does not establish an effective fertility treatment or a routine screening indication.

Should everyone take progesterone for a suspected short luteal phase?

No. Diagnosis and natural-cycle benefit are uncertain. Prescribed progesterone in a treatment protocol is a separate situation to discuss with the treating clinician.

Do the untreated-birth statistics mean I should keep waiting?

They cannot make that decision for you. Age, duration, findings and preferences should guide a defined plan rather than an indefinite delay.

Can treatment help without finding a cause?

It may. Your clinician can explain options intended to improve conception chances, their evidence and the risks, while acknowledging what remains unknown.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
